elements.element: No liquidated damages are payable by Customer under any trigger or circumstance.
elements.evidence: The rendered clause prohibits liquidated damages only “for any delay in providing a dependency”; it does not establish a general prohibition on liquidated damages payable by Customer.

elements.element: No penalties are payable by Customer under any trigger or circumstance.
elements.evidence: The rendered clause prohibits penalties only “for any delay in providing a dependency”; it does not establish a general prohibition on penalties payable by Customer.

elements.element: Any liquidated amount payable by Customer may arise only as an early-termination fee.
elements.evidence: The clause does not limit all liquidated amounts to an early-termination fee; it addresses only amounts arising from dependency delays.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee payable by Customer is capped at three months’ fees.
elements.evidence: No early-termination fee is imposed by the rendered clause, so the condition requiring a cap is absent.

elements.element: The early-termination fee is the sole liquidated amount payable by Customer, with no other liquidated damages or penalties payable.
elements.evidence: The clause does not state that an early-termination fee is the sole liquidated amount and does not prohibit liquidated damages or penalties outside dependency delays.

result.reason: The redline removes the USD 25,000-per-day dependency-delay charge, but its prohibition remains limited to dependency delays. It therefore does not implement the preferred blanket prohibition or the fallback’s exclusive early-termination-fee structure. A complete preferred revision would remove the limiting trigger, e.g., “Customer shall not be liable for or required to pay any liquidated damages or penalties.”
